statements.text: There's the economic transformation, which can be profound. There's safety concerns. [...] I've come to the conclusion that we absolutely have to have an agency. [...] But I believe that unless we have an agency that is going to address these questions from social media and AI, we really don't have much of a defense against the bad stuff, and the bad stuff will come.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on AI oversight, featuring testimony from tech executives including OpenAI's Sam Altman.

statements.text: You don't build an AI system without getting a license that gets tested independently.
statements.context: Senator Welch speaks during a Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on AI oversight.

statements.text: All right. Let me stop for a second, because what I am hearing you say is, it is really, really difficult to define, which I think it is, but your conclusion is we cannot do anything. I mean, the issue with AI is not just AI, it is just the amplification of the deception. You know, something that happened to Senator Fischer is so toxic to trust in the political system, and that is getting out of control as it is. [...] How do we deal with this? Then second, what is your observation about the platforms like Twitter, now X, Google, Facebook, essentially laying off all the folks whose job it was within those organizations to be reviewing this material that is so dangerous for democracy?
statements.context: Senator Welch speaks during a hearing on AI and the Future of Our Elections, questioning an expert witness about political disinformation and platform moderation.

statements.text: There is a lot of opportunity with AI. [...] The big question I have about AI is with the entry cost. How can we do things that are going to help the smaller farmers get the benefit of AI when they are just not going to be able to take that risk about the high upfront cost.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI in agriculture, where Senator Welch questions a witness about cost barriers for small farms.

statements.text: Let me put a little ripple on it too, because in addition to that, the smaller farmers, a lot of times will be wanting to do this, focus on profitability and value added products. The data that goes into the AI algorithm is essentially generated by the larger operations. How is that going to make it more difficult for the smaller farms that have a different business model, in effect, to be able to take benefit of AI? How do we integrate that into the systems?
statements.context: Senate hearing titled Innovation in American Agriculture: Leveraging Technology and Artificial Intelligence.

statements.text: Can you discuss some of the risks surrounding the data collection, and whether or not and why you think a user should have to give their express informed consent before an AI system harvests their data?
statements.context: Senator Welch questioning a witness during a Senate Judiciary subcommittee hearing on algorithms, competition, and consumer rights.

statements.text: One of the big concerns that all of us have, really, is meaningful consumer notification and consent and how individual information is being used, and as I understand it large language models are training on massive data sets scraped from all across the Internet and that can include private and personally identifiable information.
statements.context: Senate hearing on consumer privacy and AI, where Senator Welch questions witnesses about data consent and introduces his legislative proposal.

statements.text: Senator Bennet and I have introduced the Digital Commission—the Digital Platform Commission Act, and what it would do is establish an independent Federal commission to regulate digital platforms and that would include on key issues like AI and privacy concerns. [...] Congress simply cannot keep up with everything that is happening and we cannot address everything in a one-off piece of legislation.
statements.context: Senate hearing titled 'The Need to Protect Americans' Privacy and the AI Accelerant,' where Senator Welch questions a witness about his proposed legislation.

statements.text: It is a Republican-led bill that strips States of their right to pass laws to protect their consumers against AI threats and against social media threats. [...] It imposes a moratorium for 10 years on any States taking any action. This affects Vermont directly. It affects every single one of our States.
statements.context: Rep. Welch speaks on the House floor against a budget reconciliation bill that includes a federal moratorium on state AI and social media regulations.

statements.text: The AI companies need content, so they don't care where it comes from. It is just a voracious, insatiable appetite.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on AI companies' use of copyrighted works for AI training.

statements.text: And we just can't allow that. You know, that is just really wrong. Thank you. So we are in agreement here that we need some reforms here to protect the artist.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Committee hearing examining AI companies' use of copyrighted works for model training.

statements.text: It is only a matter of time—and probably far less time than we think—before the application of AI technology to warfare creates a whole new impetus for global instability. But even as AI becomes more versatile as a disruptive and destructive force, nuclear weapons and the threat of nuclear war are not going to disappear.
statements.context: Senate floor speech by Senator Peter Welch urging renewal of the New START nuclear arms control treaty, with a closing warning about AI's destabilizing potential in warfare.
